key_insight: A self-supervised graph transformer learns cell representations from imaging-based spatial transcriptomics and identifies spatial single-cell interactions directly—without needing predefined ligand–receptor pairs or large gene panels.
problem_solved: Overcomes limited gene panels and reliance on known ligand–receptor annotations that hinder accurate inference of cell–cell interactions from imaging-based spatial transcriptomics.
method: Build a spatial graph where nodes = single cells (from imaging) and edges encode neighborhood proximity.
Self-supervised pretraining (e.g., masked/contrastive objectives) to learn robust cell embeddings from limited gene panels and spatial context.
Graph transformer leverages attention across the spatial graph to predict pairwise interactions and produces interpretable interaction scores without ligand–receptor priors.
impact: Enables discovery of biologically meaningful cell–cell interactions from sparse spatial data using modern graph and self-supervised techniques, offering transferable representations and interpretable attention-based interaction maps useful for downstream biological analysis and scaffold-building in spatial-omics ML pipelines.
visual_elements: Tissue image overlaid with a spatial cell graph (nodes and proximity edges) to show input construction
Schematic of the graph transformer + self-supervised objective (masked/contrastive) highlighting attention flow
Attention/interaction heatmap at single-cell resolution mapped back onto tissue to show inferred interactions

paper_title: Identifying spatial single-cell-level interactions with graph transformer
